messages.subject: Ridge regression
parts:
Hi to all,

I looked at this example about ridge regression and tried to understand what exactly happens here. It's not completely documented, but maybe I am already right with my strategy.

To describe my problem:

The basic model is to describe the expression activity of two alleles by:  <expression level> = <activity allele 1>*<count of allele 1> + <activity allele 2>*<count of allele 2>  ; no intercept!!!!

Now I would like to see whether a second gene influences the expression level. For this purpose, I add this ridge term:
<expression level> ~ <count of allele 1> + <count of allele 2>  + f(beta1, <count of influencing allele 1>, model="iid", values=c(1,2)) + f(beta2, <count of influencing allele 2>, copy="beta1")
... compare the example ...

But what happens now? What am I specifying with the <count of influencing allele 1> etc.? A weight vector?
And I do something else: <count of influencing allele 1> + <count of influencing allele 2> := constant positive, and the coefficients are not necessarily pairwise positive and negative ... so my question is: do I have some intrinsic intercept, that the "iid" term does not is balanced to 0?

I tried something weird, to include an intercept term as f(beta3, <intercept>, copy="beta1"), with <intercept> representing an "always 1" vector ... but it seems not to be necessary, as it is about 0+/-1e-9?

Can you help me understanding this R-INLA function?

Best,
Andreas

messages.author: 673086e375eccf25
messages.subject: Re: Ridge regression
parts:
Hi,

to describe the math of the model better:

y: vector of gene expression level
x1, x2: vector of counts of allels for genes (in the regular case: x1+x2:=2)

To estimate the amount of gene expression produced by x1 and x2, the model y ~ x1 + x2 + 0 is to be solved.

Now I would like to see whether some additional information of influencing genes can be included.I can see that another gene (w with alleles w1 and w2, but w1+w2 is not constant 2 ) leads to a nearly linear increase of y (compare attached figure), even if the mRNA of this gene is not detected (!!!), so I would change the model to:

y ~ x1 + x2 + 0  + [w1 + w2 + an_intercept_to_balance_influence_of_gene_w]

the term in squared brackets should be centered around 0. It might be, that it is not centered around 0, but if there is no influence of Gene w, then this term should not lead to a model like this:

y ~ x1 + x2 + 1 ... because x1 and x2 are both 100% inversely correlated, an intercept in this model would lead to bad results.

What I now tried was the following idea: w1, w2 and this intercept for w all come from a common distribution N(0, sigma^2). This is expressed by the ridge term ... by this, sigma^2 will be as small as possible, if
there is no explanatory value in gene w. The principle behind ridging - as far as I understood it here - is to assume that all coefficients are small.

So: the model worked, but I was asking myself whether it is necessary to formulate it for INLA together with this intercept. The alternatives I see are:

f(beta1, w1, model="iid", values=c(1,2,3)) + f(beta2, w2, copy="beta1") + f(beta3, intercept_w, copy="beta1")

or

f(beta1, w1, model="iid", values=c(1,2)) + f(beta2, w2, copy="beta1")    no intercept

The result was, with both approaches, that the coeffients for x1 and x2 stayed the same, but I found a relevant coeffienct for w1, while w2 and intercept were nearly 0.

****
Then I became more tough and tried to combine more ridged terms to determine whether different "aspects" of gene w are important.

I have a copy numbered gene, so w1 + w2 = sum(w) ; w1 and w2 describe here alleles which differ at a SNP at position A. w1_B and w2_B do the same, but describe SNP at position B.
w1_B is not equal to w1, but w1 + w2 = w1_B + w2_b = ...

Now I added the following multiple ridging terms:

f(beta1, w1, model="iid", values=c(1,2,3)) + f(beta2, w2, copy="beta1") + f(beta3, intercept_w, copy="beta1")  +
  f(alpha1, w1_B, model="iid", values=c(1,2,3)) + f(alpha2, w2_B, copy="alpha1") + f(alpha3, intercept_w_B, copy="alpha1")

I can calculate the model for all ridging terms separately, and they are staying nearly the same, which speaks for the stability of this approach. In addition, I see that the alpha model above leads to very small variance
for the iid model, while for beta it is much bigger. I am not sure that this means the alpha term is not as important as the beta term.

***

messages.subject: Re: Ridge regression
parts:
Hi,

think I slowly understand the whole concepts. In fact, it is very much what I described in another thread: http://www.r-inla.org/comments-1?place=topic%2Fr-inla-discussion-group%2F1G83cc6dRnA%2Fdiscussion

For any binomial or linear regression, alleles of single genes are used as covariates. If, however, a certain allele is not very frequent, the posterior distribution tends to have a too large variation. Or in other words: if allele A has a log OR of 1.3 +/- 0.5, allele B -1.3 +/-0.5, then the very rare allele C is unlikely to have a log OR of 0 +/- 100 ... only as an example. It is better and more to assume that log odds ratios are coming from a common Gaussian distribution.
In the thread  above, the undocumented model "z" is recommended. However: it seems to be better to use the concept described in the "stacks" example for ridging!

The mathematics in the model I thought about in this thread is in fact a little weird. The idea came, because I saw a tendency of the ridge regression to somehow "squeeze" the posterior distributions of ridged covariates to a zero-variance Gaussian distribution, if there is no relevant information in these covariates that explain the response variable. Inclusion of an "intercept" into the group of ridged covariates was therefore a very dirty approach.

The figure attached shows better what I think about the reality behind .... text boxes are (latent) variables, arrows show (the most important) feed-back and feed-forward influences, that might be modeled as functions of corresponding variables. My response variable is "MRNA Gene 1" expression levels, which is product of alleles A, B and C of gene 1. Specific activity for gene 1, i.e. transcription activation or inhibition for gene 1, is stimulated by gene 2 protein products. "Spontaneous source of activity" is the [partly structured] noise. Maybe it is not possible to express this whole model with R-INLA.Ideas?

If tried to do the modeling, to express mRNA as response variable in a linear regression, with gene 1 alleles as covariates, and gene 2 alleles as ridged covariates.
With MCMC, I would just model all influences and (latent) variables as a bunch of interconnected functions that finally calculate the response variable.

Best,
Andreas

messages.subject: Re: Ridge regression
parts:
Hi, I tried to figure how to express the problem depicted in the schematic.
It is mainly a "simple linear regression", where the coefficients are split up into two components - an individual and a common one - which are then multiplied.
y is here the mRNA level, x_i the number of alleles of gene 1, f(r_i) some random factor function, z_i the number of alleles of the influencing gene 2.

The common component exp(v) is the result of another linear regression that contains random and fixed effects.

To compare it with the schematic: exp(v) is the specific activity (light blue), which activates alleles of gene 1. This specific activity multiplies the individual expression rate of every allele of gene 1.

Maybe it is possible to reformulate that model. Could it be that the "weights" parameter in the formulation "f(x, weights, model, ..)" can be of help? Or is it simply not possible to do it?
